docs.title: About
docs.text:
I have supervised excavation for boundary compliance in Riau, measured forest plots for an above-ground biomass study on peatland, and digitized land cover from satellite imagery at RECOFTC. I use QGIS, ArcGIS, Google Earth Engine, and Python with Pandas and Matplotlib.

I have also counted oil palms from UAV orthophotos (Palm Tree Counting), measured how often Sentinel-1 sees a flood while it is rising (Flood Coverage), and built a quality checker for GBIF species records (BioSift). I mapped surface heat and vegetation change in Pekanbaru (Urban Surface Temperature, Urban Green Space Change).

I am looking for entry-level roles in GIS analysis, remote sensing, or environmental data work, preferably connected to forest monitoring.

Portrait / undercover field operative, Riau, 2026

docs.title: BioSift
docs.text: Plate 01 · quality report and map view · GBIF occurrence records scored against ten checks

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
BioSift is an open-source web app for checking species occurrence records from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF). Before a GBIF dataset is used for analysis, it helps to know whether coordinates are missing or misplaced, whether records are duplicated, and where coverage gaps are. BioSift runs those checks. Enter one or more species names, set a year range, and the app fetches the records from the GBIF API, scores them, and reports the results.

Study area: Global Year: 2026 Role: Solo project Status: Completed; submitted to the 2026 GBIF Ebbe Nielsen Challenge

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data source

  • GBIF.org occurrence records, retrieved through the public API

Processing steps

  1. Fetch occurrence data from the GBIF API with filters for year range, basis of record, and record limit
  2. Run ten automated quality checks: missing coordinates, zero coordinates, duplicate records, coordinate-country mismatch, low coordinate precision, and temporal gap detection
  3. Produce spatial diagnostics: an interactive point map, heatmaps, DBSCAN-based outlier detection, and a Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) preview of the species distribution
  4. Score each record for reliability on a 0–100 scale and rate the dataset's fitness for five scientific use cases
  5. Export results as CSV, reliability-scored CSV, or a Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A)

Tools

Tool Purpose Python + Streamlit Web application pygbif GBIF API access pandas Data cleaning and filtering folium + plotly Interactive maps and charts scikit-learn DBSCAN spatial outlier detection scipy Kernel Density Estimation

docs.title: Occurrence Map
docs.text: Interactive point map with clean records (green) and flagged records (red).

docs.title: Temporal Analysis
docs.text: Records per year with a trend line, showing how collection effort has changed over time.

docs.title: Charts & Statistics
docs.text: Country observation density, basis of record breakdown, and coordinate precision tiers.

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text: Global data gap map on a 10° grid, with alerts for cells with little or no coverage.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Runs ten quality checks and summarizes each dataset with a data health score from 0 to 100%
  • Compares up to five species side by side and exports the comparison as a report
  • Generates a methods paragraph and GBIF dataset citations in APA or BibTeX format
  • Exports cleaned records as CSV or Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A)
  • Runs in the browser with no installation; the source code is public

docs.title: Flood Coverage
docs.text: Plate 01 · coverage figures for the four basins · one year of Sentinel-1 acquisition metadata

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Flood maps show where water was. Flood Coverage asks whether a satellite would see a flood while it is rising.

Public flood mapping has largely solved speed. Copernicus GFM publishes a global 20 m flood layer in under eight hours for more than 99% of scenes, and the fastest documented activation delivered its first extent eight hours after trigger. The remaining limit is how rarely the satellite looks, compared with how fast the water moves. A basin can be called monitored while a short flood passes entirely between two passes.

The project measures that gap from acquisition metadata and pairs the result with the free GloFAS discharge forecast for each basin, to ask whether a forecast peak can be checked by a satellite pass.

Study areas Po river plain (IT), Ahr valley (DE), Siak (Riau, ID), Ciliwung (Jakarta, ID) Period 1 November 2025 to 1 November 2026 Role Solo project Status Working analysis and demo, source public

docs.title: The measurement
docs.text:
The probability is computed empirically, not modelled. Take the acquisition timestamps for a year, slide a rise window across them in one hour steps, and count how often a look falls inside the window.

P(rise observed) = windows containing at least one look / all windows

Passes cluster, so the answer differs sharply from the nominal revisit figure. The same run also reports the gap distribution, so any rise time can be read off without re-running.

docs.title: Results, one year and one collection
docs.text:
Basin Looks per year Looks per day Median gap 6 h rise seen 48 h rise seen Po, Italy 315 0.87 24.0 h 21% 91% Ahr, Germany 250 0.69 24.0 h 17% 91% Siak, Riau 78 0.22 120.1 h 5% 39% Ciliwung, Jakarta 51 0.14 203.3 h 3% 28%

The Po and the Ahr have almost the same cadence, 0.87 and 0.69 looks per day and a 24 hour median gap, and they land in completely different places: 90% against 17% at a six hour rise. The satellites are the same; the basins rise at different speeds. Jakarta's median gap of 203 hours means a flash flood is essentially never observed while it is rising, and its longest blackout in the year ran 288 hours, from 22 September to 4 October 2026.

docs.title: Can the forecast be checked?
docs.text:
GloFAS already issues a free 30 day river discharge forecast for every basin here. Each forecast peak is paired with the measured chance that a look lands within 24 hours of it.

Basin Forecast peak Date (2026) Versus 30 day median Checkable within a day Po 2746.9 m³/s 22 Nov 3.2x 91% Ahr 5.7 m³/s 15 Nov 6.8x 91% Siak, Riau 447.8 m³/s 23 Nov 3.6x 39% Ciliwung, Jakarta 34.0 m³/s 24 Nov 4.8x 28%

Europe can check its own forecast. Jakarta cannot: for 72% of forecast peaks no look lands within a day, so the forecast is issued and acted on without being checked.

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data sources

  • Sentinel-1 GRD acquisition metadata, queried through the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API
  • GloFAS v4 river discharge forecast, through the Open-Meteo forecast API
  • Esri World Dark Gray basemap, for the locator map only

Processing steps

  1. Search the STAC API for each basin's bounding box over the 12 month window
  2. Deduplicate polarisation pairs so each overpass counts once
  3. Compute the gap distribution, the median and 95th percentile gap, and the count of gaps over 48 hours
  4. Slide the rise window across the record in one hour steps to estimate the observation probability at 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 72 and 168 hours
  5. Pull the GloFAS forecast per basin on a 3x3 sampling grid, keeping the cell with the highest median discharge, because the basin centroid often falls on a headwater cell
  6. Pair each forecast peak with the measured probability that a look falls within 24 hours of it

Tools

Tool Purpose Python standard library Ingest, statistics, and the web server STAC API (HTTP + JSON) Sentinel-1 acquisition metadata Open-Meteo API GloFAS discharge forecast HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript The page, with no build step MapLibre GL JS Locator map of the basin boxes

The analysis runs on the Python standard library alone: no dependencies, no API keys, no build step. Every statistic on the page is computed locally from the downloaded metadata.

docs.title: The app
docs.text:
• Shows, per basin, the share of randomly timed floods of a chosen rise length that contain at least one acquisition
  • Draws the whole sweep from 3 to 168 hours, so the conclusion can be read at any rise time instead of resting on one assumption
  • Renders the full year as a strip, one tick per acquisition, with every gap drawn at its true length
  • Reports the longest blackout in the year and how many separate floods would fit inside it
  • Pairs today's GloFAS forecast peak with the measured chance that it can be confirmed by a look

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No acquisition is not no flood. A gap means no look, not absent water, and nothing is rendered as zero.
  • Rise times are assumptions, not per-event measurements, which is why the page shows the full sweep.
  • GloFAS covers rivers only, on a grid that does not resolve small steep catchments, and it is not a flood warning.
  • The four basins are not a global sample. Both European basins sit inside the acquisition scenario that plans them for frequent revisit, and the Indonesian pair shows how far below that coverage can fall.
  • This is a personal analysis, not a peer reviewed study.

docs.title: Palm Tree Counting
docs.text: Plate 01 · merged mosaic, block 47N · 0.155 m ground pixel

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Counting oil palms by hand from aerial imagery is slow. A single block of a few hundred hectares holds tens of thousands of crowns, and the count has to be redone whenever a block is replanted, thinned, or audited.

This project counts them automatically. Five UAV orthophotos covering just over 310 hectares are merged into one mosaic, the mosaic is resampled to the ground resolution the detector was trained at, a YOLOv8 model runs inference on a free GPU in Google Colab, and the detections come back as georeferenced points that carry a confidence value and a crown size in metres. The points then go into ordinary GIS analysis. Here that means counting how many trees fall inside a 500 m river setback and inside the 5 m river polygons themselves.

The run produced 24,966 trees over 310.8 hectares, a density of 80.3 trees per hectare.

Study area Oil palm blocks in Riau, Indonesia (UTM zones 47N and 48N) Imagery UAV orthophotos, 0.071 m to 0.155 m ground pixel Year 2026 Role Solo project Status Pipeline complete, source public

docs.title: Merge before detecting
docs.text: When orthophotos overlap, detecting each file separately counts every tree in the overlap twice, and the total inflates by however much the files share. The inputs are therefore merged into a single raster first, so each point on the ground is visited once. The output grid is snapped to the pixel grid of the sharpest source rather than to the union of all extents, which keeps that source free of resampling blur, and the mosaic is written lossless with overviews so a multi gigapixel file still pans smoothly in QGIS.

docs.title: Match the ground resolution
docs.text: A detector only recognises objects at the scale it learned. The model was trained on 640 pixel tiles at 0.155 m ground pixel, which is 99 m of ground per tile. On the 0.071 m orthophoto the same tile covers only 46 m, so every tree appears twice as large and accuracy falls even though the image is sharper. The imagery is resampled to 0.155138 m before inference, which also cuts the work: the tile count on that block dropped from roughly 3,300 to 735.

docs.title: Overlapping tiles, one global deduplication
docs.text: The mosaic is cut into strips locally, then processed as overlapping square tiles on the GPU. Overlap is kept large because a crown on a tile edge would otherwise be seen only partially. Transparent gaps between flight corridors are skipped using the alpha band, raw boxes are filtered by confidence, and non maximum suppression removes duplicate boxes. That is not enough in a regularly planted orchard, where two strong boxes can land on one crown, so a final spatial filter removes any detection closer than a minimum distance to a stronger one. The distance comes from the expected planting spacing, and it is applied across the whole dataset rather than per tile, which is what closes the leakage at strip boundaries.

docs.title: One row per tree
docs.text: Each surviving box becomes its centre point, with the box dimensions converted from pixels to metres using the raster resolution. The points are written as GeoPackage, GeoJSON and CSV in the CRS of the input imagery, so crown size statistics arrive for free and every detection can be reviewed in QGIS before it is used.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Source Valid area Trees Density Median confidence Mosaic of four orthos (47N) 310.8 ha 24,966 80.3 /ha 0.697 ORTO 47N, run as its own file 138.1 ha 12,864 93.1 /ha PMBN1 47N 63.5 ha 6,008 94.6 /ha 0.755 PMBN3 47N 48.2 ha 399 8.3 /ha 0.633 PMBN ORTO2 (tagged 48S, actually 48N) 90.2 ha 8,040 89.1 /ha 0.704

The low density on PMBN3 comes from the block itself, not a detection failure: it holds far fewer palms over a similar area than its neighbours.

docs.title: Detector accuracy
docs.text:
The model is a YOLOv8 nano fine tuned on a public Roboflow Universe dataset of 2,730 images and 180,170 boxes, and evaluated on a 280 image validation split from that same dataset.

Metric Value mAP@50 0.977 Precision / recall 0.955 / 0.955 mAP@50-95 0.745 F1 at IoU 0.5 on a production check 0.814 (recall 84.6%, precision 78.5%) Count bias in production use plus or minus 8% Agreement with an independent digitising pass 92%

The first three rows describe the public dataset, not these blocks. The count bias and the 92% agreement are the numbers that apply to the plantation imagery.

docs.title: The same trees, counted two ways
docs.text:
Detecting each orthophoto separately and detecting the merged mosaic once should give the same answer. Checking that shows whether the mosaic step changes the count:

Source Per ortho On mosaic Difference ORTO 47N 93.1 /ha 93.0 /ha -0.1% PMBN1 47N 94.6 /ha 98.8 /ha +4.4% PMBN ORTO2 (48N) 89.1 /ha 86.9 /ha -2.5%

docs.title: River setback analysis
docs.text:
Three of the orthophotos were tested against a 500 m setback shapefile and 5 m wide river polygons, as a demonstration that the point layer is analysis ready and not just a picture.

Item Value Trees inside the 500 m setback 2,253 of 6,495 Trees inside the 5 m river polygons 100, across 6 river segments Setback clip area per ortho 20.8 / 5.3 / 20.0 ha River clip area per ortho 1.05 / 0.27 / 1.02 ha

No reprojection is needed for this step, because the points and the zones share a CRS. The same scripts clip the source rasters to each zone so the counts can be checked.

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data sources

  • UAV orthophotos in RGB with an alpha band, five files across UTM zones 47N and 48N
  • A public oil palm detection dataset on Roboflow Universe for fine tuning, 2,730 images and 180,170 boxes
  • 500 m river setback and 5 m river polygon shapefiles, supplied as vector zones

Processing steps

  1. Merge the orthophotos into one lossless mosaic on a grid snapped to the sharpest source
  2. Resample to the 0.155138 m ground sample distance used in training
  3. Cut the mosaic into strips, then run overlapping tile inference on a Colab T4 GPU with the alpha band masking empty ground
  4. Deduplicate detections globally by confidence and minimum planting distance, then convert boxes to centre points with crown dimensions in metres
  5. Export to GeoPackage, GeoJSON and CSV, and render every detection back onto the imagery for a visual check
  6. Count points inside the setback and river polygons, and clip the rasters to those zones

Tools

Tool Purpose Python The whole pipeline, run as scripts GDAL / OGR (osgeo) Mosaicking, resampling, raster and vector I/O Ultralytics YOLOv8 + PyTorch Detector training and inference Google Colab, T4 GPU Free GPU for training and tile inference NumPy, SciPy Raster arrays, morphology, spatial filtering QGIS Visual review of detections and zone counts

A CRS error in one file. The second block's orthophoto is tagged WGS 84 / UTM zone 48S with a false northing of 10,000,000, but its coordinates resolve to 0°21' N, north of the equator in zone 48N. As tagged, the file sits in the wrong hemisphere, so its CRS was corrected before it was used with the others. The pipeline checks CRS and ground resolution before inference because an error like that is invisible until a layer lands in the wrong place.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• There are no ground plots. The plus or minus 8% is count bias on a labelled validation split plus run to run consistency, not a field measurement. Narrowing it needs stems counted on the ground.
  • The 0.977 mAP belongs to the public training dataset. It says the model learned that data well, not that it scores the same on these blocks.
  • In the densest rows, touching crowns with no contrast between them merge into one detection, so recall is the weak side there. A stricter separation threshold splits more of them and lowers the count.
  • A tree count is not tree health, age, or yield. Crown area is measured, nothing about the palm itself is.
  • The plantation imagery is not public, so the repository ships the pipeline and a sample of the output rather than the results themselves.
  • Positions are only as good as the orthophoto's georeferencing. The pipeline inherits it and cannot improve on it.

docs.title: Species Distribution Model Comparison
docs.text: Plate 01 · three species, spatial block CV · AUC and TSS, bars are one SD over folds

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Four algorithms are used here to predict where a species can occur from climate: maximum entropy (MaxEnt), random forest, an RBF support vector machine and XGBoost. Reports often compare them across different datasets, which mixes the algorithm with the data. This project holds the data fixed and changes only the model.

Presences come from GBIF, thinned to one record per 10 arc minute cell. Climate comes from WorldClim 2.1 at the same resolution, pruned to the variables that are not collinear at |r| > 0.8. All four models get the same 2,000 background cells, the same predictors and the same folds, so a difference in the table is a difference between models.

Each model is scored twice: once with stratified random 5-fold and once with spatial block 5-fold on a 5 by 5 grid. The second scheme is the reference, because random folds let neighbouring records fall into different folds and measure interpolation between them.

Study area Europe (Quercus robur, Ursus arctos) and the Namib (Welwitschia mirabilis) Projection WGS 84, WorldClim 2.1 at 10 arc minutes (about 18 km) Source GBIF occurrence records; WorldClim 2.1 bioclim and elevation Records 9,000 pulled per species where available, then thinned to one per grid cell Role Solo project Status Complete, source public

docs.title: The comparison
docs.text:
Spatial block cross-validation, five folds. AUC is rank based. TSS uses a threshold fitted on a held-out 30 percent calibration split inside each training fold, so it is never tuned on the data the model was fitted to.

Species Presences SVM (RBF) Random forest MaxEnt XGBoost Quercus robur 1,835 0.782 / 0.430 0.813 / 0.464 0.808 / 0.480 0.807 / 0.437 Ursus arctos 1,418 0.833 / 0.436 0.856 / 0.516 0.835 / 0.495 0.844 / 0.517 Welwitschia mirabilis 91 0.590 / 0.072 0.654 / 0.116 0.725 / 0.152 0.492 / 0.149

Cells read as AUC / TSS, bold marks the best value in the row.

On the oak, with 1,835 presences and ten predictors, the four models sit within 0.031 AUC and 0.05 TSS of each other. MaxEnt has the highest TSS, random forest the highest AUC. At that sample size the gap is fold noise, and the four predictions support the same description of the species' climatic niche.

The 91-record case is different. The spread there is 0.233 AUC. MaxEnt holds 0.725 and XGBoost falls to 0.492, which is chance: 400 boosting rounds exceed what that dataset can support, and one of the five blocks held too few presences to score, so the species is averaged over four folds with a standard deviation of 0.299. The SVM fails in a different way. It predicted the whole extent suitable (area fraction 1.000), so its TSS of 0.072 comes from calling everything present.

docs.title: What random folds would have said
docs.text:
Model Mean AUC, random folds Mean AUC, spatial blocks Inflation MaxEnt 0.890 0.789 +0.101 Random forest 0.885 0.774 +0.111 SVM (RBF) 0.865 0.735 +0.131 XGBoost 0.883 0.715 +0.168

Every model loses between 0.10 and 0.17 AUC when neighbouring records are kept in the same fold, and the flexible learners lose the most. A comparison built on random folds puts XGBoost above MaxEnt; under spatial blocks the order reverses. That reversal is the result I would flag to anyone reading an SDM paper that reports random-fold AUC only.

The learning curves locate where each model starts to work. MaxEnt is at 0.707 AUC with 50 oak presences and 0.784 with all of them, while random forest climbs from 0.636 to 0.774 over the same range.

docs.title: Which algorithm fits which data situation
docs.text: Situation Start with Why, from this panel Under about 100 usable presences MaxEnt 0.725 against 0.492 to 0.654 here, and it is the only model whose predictions are not degenerate at that size 100 to 500 presences MaxEnt, then random forest the curves cross near 100; both are defensible, and random forest has lower variance across folds once it has data Several thousand presences Random forest or MaxEnt 0.813 against 0.808 on the oak; pick on what the output is for, not on AUC Clustered, fragmented records Random forest 0.856 on the bear, the highest in the panel A probability for policy or reporting MaxEnt cloglog output on a 0 to 1 scale; tree vote fractions are not probabilities Prediction into a novel climate MaxEnt clamping limits extrapolation, and trees cannot extrapolate at all

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Processing steps

  1. Query GBIF for accepted records with coordinates, no fatal geospatial issue, present status, since 1950, and fetch pages in parallel up to 9,000 records per species
  2. Apply seven quality gates in order (coordinate validity, study extent, GBIF issue flags, basis of record, year, stated uncertainty, duplicate coordinates) and record how many records each gate removes
  3. Thin to one record per 10 arc minute cell, keeping the best located record
  4. Clip WorldClim 2.1 bioclim and elevation to the extent and drop variables correlated above |r| = 0.8, leaving ten predictors shared by every model
  5. Draw 2,000 background cells once per species and pass them to all four models, including MaxEnt, which normally samples its own
  6. Fit the four models with fixed hyperparameters and score each under random and spatial block folds, with TSS taken from a calibration split inside each training fold

Tools

Tool Purpose Python: scikit-learn random forest, RBF SVM, XGBoost wrapper, GroupKFold maxent.jar 3.4.4 reference MaxEnt build, driven from a subprocess pygbif, requests occurrence retrieval from the GBIF API rasterio, rioxarray WorldClim clipping, ASCII grids for MaxEnt, prediction stacks pandas, Matplotlib tables, figures, provenance record

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• 10 arc minute resolution sets a floor on what can be modelled. A first candidate, Nepenthes rajah, had 80 records at a stated 31 km precision, which left two grid cells after thinning, so it was replaced by Welwitschia mirabilis.
  • 9,000 records is a cap, not the population. The oak has 1.7 million records available, and the search API stalls beyond about 10,000 offsets, so the cap is recorded in the provenance file.
  • One background size, no bias correction. Sampling effort is uneven in reality, and no target-group background is used.
  • Hyperparameters are fixed a priori so tuning cannot leak into the comparison, which means the table measures each algorithm's default behaviour rather than its best.
  • AUC compares models within a species, never across species, because the extent and the background differ between cases.
  • MaxEnt needs a display even in batch mode, so the remote Colab runner selects the three scikit-learn models instead.

docs.title: Urban Green Space Change
docs.text: Plate 01 · Kota Pekanbaru boundary, UTM 47N · 20 m NDVI change, 2019 to 2025

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Pekanbaru has grown into surrounding forest, plantation and peat. This project asks which ground lost vegetation, which gained it, and what land cover was there when the change happened.

Two calendar years of Sentinel-2 surface reflectance are compared on the city boundary itself, at the 20 m resolution of the cloud mask. Cloud is handled per pixel from the Sentinel-2 classification layer, and pixels without at least five clear observations in both years are dropped rather than averaged over whatever survived.

Study area Kota Pekanbaru, Riau (FAO GAUL 2025 boundary), 62,884 ha Projection WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647), 20 m Source Sentinel-2 L2A surface reflectance, SCL cloud mask Periods 2019 (43 scenes) and 2025 (39 scenes) Role Solo project Status Analysis complete, source public

docs.title: Why 20 m, and why whole years
docs.text:
The Sentinel-2 classification layer that carries the cloud flag is native at 20 m. Analysing at 10 m would mean interpolating the mask, so 20 m is the finest grid where the mask is an observation rather than a guess.

Each period is a median of every clear observation in the calendar year. The composite is built per pixel, so a scene that is cloudy over the city but clear over the rest of the tile is not thrown away, and about 15 clear observations per pixel survive on average.

A pixel is analysed only if it has at least five clear observations in both periods and is not permanent water, so the city mean is a land figure and not a river statistic. That leaves 62,110 ha, or 98.8% of the city.

docs.title: Change classes and attribution
docs.text: Change is classified at plus or minus 0.03 NDVI, roughly the noise floor between two clear composites, and the areas come from summing pixel area rather than multiplying a pixel count by a nominal size. Every analysed pixel is then labelled with ESA WorldCover 2021 and the classes are cross-tabulated, so the attribution totals reconcile with the headline.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Mean NDVI rose from 0.576 to 0.605 (+0.028). The class table below separates loss, stable ground, and gain.

2019 2025 Change Mean NDVI 0.576 0.605 +0.028 Median NDVI 0.668 0.707 +0.039 Scenes used 43 39 n/a Class (change above 0.10 NDVI) Area (ha) Share Loss 6,356 10.2% Stable 41,436 66.7% Gain 14,318 23.1% Net +7,962

docs.title: Where the change happened
docs.text:
Tree cover carries most of both sides: 4,750 ha lost and 10,234 ha gained, a net +5,485 ha. Built-up land shows 2,468 ha of gain against 826 ha of loss, which is more plausibly canopy and garden vegetation inside settlements than new buildings, since the built-up class includes vegetated urban surfaces.

The clearest single loss is a 270 ha rectilinear block in the east of the city at 101.557 E, 0.592 N, where composite NDVI fell from 0.701 to 0.509. It held 17.2 and 15.1 clear observations per pixel in the two periods, so it is a real change rather than a cloud gap, and edges that straight are the signature of plantation block clearing rather than gradual urban creep.

docs.title: 2019 was a low starting point
docs.text: Running the composite for every year shows the two comparison years in context: NDVI climbs from 0.572 to a 2022 peak of 0.624 and then flattens to about 0.600. Part of the 2019 to 2025 increase is recovery from a dry, fire-affected 2019 in Riau, not a sustained greening trend. The 2022 to 2025 decline of about 0.025 is the more useful signal for present conditions.

docs.title: Two independent checks
docs.text:
Both checks test the result against a second sensor and a different seasonal window.

Check Result Dry-season window instead of whole years (Landsat) net -0.004, area losing 29.0% Whole-year window (Landsat) net -0.008, area losing 29.5% Sentinel-2 against Landsat per 2 km cell r = 0.45 over 182 cells (p = 2e-10)

The loss share barely moves between windows, so the loss finding is robust while the net mean is not: a mean of a bimodal change distribution is the balance of two large opposing areas, not a typical pixel. The cross-sensor comparison puts the two instruments on the same 2 km cells and finds they agree on where change happened, while Sentinel-2 reads about 0.03 NDVI higher, which matches the low 2019 baseline rather than contradicting it.

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Processing steps

  1. Filter Sentinel-2 L2A to one calendar year per period with a loose scene cloud filter, because cloud is handled per pixel afterwards
  2. Keep only SCL classes 4, 5, 6 and 11; drop shadow, cloud, cirrus, saturated and no-data
  3. Build per-pixel median NDVI for each period, with a clear-observation count per period
  4. Apply the analysis mask: at least five clear observations in both periods, and not permanent water
  5. Difference the composites, classify at plus or minus 0.03 and plus or minus 0.10, and sum pixel area for exact hectares
  6. Label every pixel with ESA WorldCover 2021 and cross-tabulate the classes against change
  7. Test the result against a seasonal window and against a second sensor

Tools

Tool Purpose Google Earth Engine composites, cloud masking, zonal statistics, pixel area Python: earthengine-api, rasterio download, raster handling NumPy, Matplotlib classification, tables, figures ESA WorldCover 2021 land-cover attribution

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• NDVI is greenness, not green space. A young oil palm block and a remnant forest can share a value and differ completely in cooling, carbon and biodiversity. A land-cover claim needs a classification, not an index.
  • NDVI saturates in dense canopy, so loss inside the most heavily forested cells is likely understated. Three of the five largest losses started above 0.75.
  • The attribution is dated mid-period. WorldCover 2021 describes the land around 2021, not its 2019 state, and plantations are labelled as tree cover, so the estate-versus-forest question stays open.
  • Two epochs are not a trend. A steady decline and a decline followed by recovery look identical here.
  • 2019 was a low, fire-affected year, which inflates any comparison that starts there.
  • The boundary is administrative, not a functional urban area.

docs.title: Urban Surface Temperature
docs.text: Plate 01 · Pekanbaru, UTM 47N · 30 m thermal, dry-season composite 2022-2024

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This project maps land surface temperature across Pekanbaru and asks which parts of the city are hottest, whether those areas also lost vegetation, and where a first round of cooling interventions would help most.

Cloud is the main problem. In the reference scene from 13 June 2023 only 43.8% of the study area was clear, and the cloud sat over the built-up ground the question is about. Dropping those pixels would leave mostly suburban ground.

The composite is built in two stages, and the page reports how much of the map comes from each.

Study area Pekanbaru, Riau, Indonesia (101.35 to 101.55 E, 0.40 to 0.60 N) Projection WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647), 30 m Source Landsat 8/9 Collection 2 Level-2, band ST_B10 Period 2022 to 2024 dry seasons Role Solo project Status Pipeline complete, source public

docs.title: How the temperature map is built
Two stages, two meanings
docs.text:
A medoid composite takes, for every pixel, the clear observation nearest the per-pixel median across 15 selected scenes. Unlike a median it is always one real reading from one real date, so no value is an average of dates. It raised clear coverage from 43.8% to 56.8% of the raster.

Large cloud blobs still had no clear observation in any of the 53 candidate scenes. For those, a linear model predicts temperature from the mean of surrounding clear pixels in a 9 by 9 window, with the pixel itself excluded from the fit so the model never trains on the value it predicts. Four passes run in sequence, each filling a ring further into the cloud, because a newly filled pixel becomes a neighbour for the next pass. Filling stops at the convex hull of everything any scene observed, so nothing is invented beyond the satellite swath.

Stage Share of raster What the value means Reference scene only 43.8% same-day observation plus medoid composite 13.0% observation from another date plus regression fill 23.1% modelled, not observed Total coverage 79.9%

docs.title: The uncertainty layer
docs.text:
Every modelled pixel carries a 1 sigma error from regression residuals pooled in a moving 25 by 25 window, so heterogeneous urban surfaces get wider bars than uniform ones. The median uncertainty across filled pixels is 0.75 K, the 95th percentile 1.43 K.

The provenance map shows where each pixel came from. Red is the reference scene, orange is an observation from another date, blue is modelled. A conclusion about a blue area is weaker than one about a red area.

docs.title: Ranking the zones
docs.text:
Each 2 km cell gets mean, minimum and maximum temperature, the share of its area that is observed rather than modelled, and a priority score:

priority = 0.6 * z(mean LST) + 0.4 * z(-ndVI change)

Hot cells score high. Cells that lost vegetation score high. Missing vegetation change counts as zero loss rather than dropping the cell, so a cell without a vegetation record can still rank on heat alone.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Across the 125 cells with data, mean land surface temperature is 35.9 °C, ranging from 27.9 °C to 43.7 °C. That is a spread of nearly 16 K inside one city, and it is not diffuse: the heat forms a contiguous core north of the Siak and a second belt along the eastern built-up corridor, with cooler ground over vegetated and peaty fringes.

Rank Cell Mean LST (°C) Change in NDVI Priority Modelled area 1 C0505 43.4 -0.006 1.40 28.7% 2 C0406 43.7 +0.001 1.19 29.2% 3 C0203 40.8 -0.014 1.16 13.2%

C0406 is the hottest cell in the city. C0505 pairs slightly lower heat with measurable vegetation loss. C0203 is the coolest of the three but lost the most vegetation, which is why it outranks hotter but greener cells.

docs.title: The vegetation result that did not behave
docs.text:
Vegetation declined in 113 of 125 cells, mean change -0.009 in NDVI. The correlation between mean temperature and vegetation change is +0.31: hotter cells tended to lose less vegetation, not more.

That sign is the opposite of the expected one. The likely explanation is that the hottest cells were already built up with little vegetation left to lose, while the largest NDVI losses happened on vegetated fringes that stay comparatively cool. NDVI change measures where vegetation disappeared, not where heat is worst. The two signals are complementary, which is why they are combined into one score instead of one being used to confirm the other.

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Processing steps

  1. Filter path 127 row 59 to 53 scenes for 2022 to 2024, score each by clear share over the area of interest, keep the best 15
  2. Mask dilated cloud, cirrus, cloud and shadow from QA_PIXEL bits 1 to 4, and treat ST_B10 = 0 as missing rather than as cold ground
  3. Convert to Celsius with the Collection 2 scaling, then build the medoid composite and keep the reference scene where it is clear
  4. Fill the remaining gaps by regression on the local neighbourhood mean, four passes, stopping at the swath boundary
  5. Compute per-pixel uncertainty and a provenance class, then zonal statistics on a 2 km grid with coverage shares
  6. Rank cells by heat and vegetation loss, and draw the plate

Tools

Tool Purpose Google Earth Engine scene selection, cloud masking, download Python: rasterio, NumPy, SciPy compositing, regression fill, zonal statistics GeoPandas, Shapely grid cells, swath hull, overlays Matplotlib plates

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The 2 km grid is not a neighbourhood. No official boundary layer was available, so cells stand in for administrative units, and real boundaries would move the zone edges.
  • This is not a single-day snapshot. The composite mixes dates, so it represents typical dry-season conditions, not the afternoon of 13 June 2023.
  • About 23% of the mapped area is modelled. Median error is 0.75 K, but a stationary regression cannot see land change between dates, so the largest filled blobs are likely worse than that number suggests.
  • Land surface temperature is not air temperature and not the heat a pedestrian feels. Dense shade can be cool at the surface while trapping heat at street level.
  • Path 127 leaves the south-west and south-east corners uncovered. Adding path 126 or 128 would close them.
  • Emissivity comes from the Landsat product and is least reliable over peatland and water.
